reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical Design - Part 1: General Rules

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Establishes that Section 11 applies to the overall stability of, and movements in, the ground -- natural or fill -- around foundations, retaining structures, natural slopes, embankments, or excavations. Overall-stability provisions specific to particular structure types are also found in Sections 6 to 10 and 12, which should be read together with this Section.
sections.body: The provisions in this Section shall apply to the overall stability of and movements in the ground, whether natural or fill, around foundations, retaining structures, natural slopes, embankments, or excavations. Account should be taken of overall stability clauses related to specific structures in Sections 6 to 10 and 12; Section 11 provides the general framework that those structure-specific clauses invoke (e.g. 9.7.2 for retaining structures, 11.5 as invoked by 12.5 for embankments).
key_points: Applies to overall stability of and movements in natural or fill ground around foundations, retaining structures, slopes, embankments, and excavations
Works together with the overall-stability clauses embedded in Sections 6 to 10 and 12
Provides the general slope/overall-stability framework invoked by structure-specific sections (e.g. Section 9's retaining-structure overall stability check, Section 12's embankment stability check)
sections.applicability: Applies to the overall (deep-seated, mass) stability of any site or structure where a failure surface could pass through the surrounding ground rather than being confined to a single structural element.

sections.title: Limit states
sections.summary: Requires that all possible limit states for the particular ground be considered to fulfil the fundamental requirements of stability, limited deformation, durability, and limits on movement of nearby structures/services. Lists three representative limit states: loss of overall stability, excessive ground movement (shear deformation, settlement, vibration, or heave), and damage or loss of serviceability in neighbouring structures, roads, or services.
sections.body: All possible limit states for the particular ground shall be considered in order to fulfil the fundamental requirements of stability, limited deformations, durability, and limitations in movements of nearby structures or services. Some possible limit states are listed: loss of overall stability of the ground and associated structures; excessive movements in the ground due to shear deformations, settlement, vibration, or heave; and damage or loss of serviceability in neighbouring structures, roads, or services due to movements in the ground.
key_points: Consider all possible limit states for the particular ground -- stability, limited deformation, durability, movement limits on nearby structures/services
Limit state: loss of overall stability of the ground and associated structures
Limit state: excessive ground movement from shear deformation, settlement, vibration, or heave
Limit state: damage or loss of serviceability in neighbouring structures, roads, or services
sections.applicability: Applies when compiling the limit-state checklist for a slope, embankment, excavation, or ground supporting a foundation or retaining structure.

sections.title: Actions and design situations
sections.summary: Lists the circumstances that overall-stability design situations must account for -- construction processes, new nearby slopes/structures, prior/continuing ground movement, vibration, climatic variation, vegetation, human/animal activity, water content/pore pressure variation, and wave action -- and requires ULS design water levels to reflect the most unfavourable hydrological conditions, including drain/filter/seal failure and, for waterfronts, steady seepage combined with rapid drawdown.
sections.body: The list in 2.4.2(4) should be taken into account when selecting the actions for calculation of limit states. The effects of the following circumstances shall be taken into account, as appropriate: construction processes; new slopes or structures on or near the particular site; previous or continuing ground movements from different sources; vibrations; climatic variations, including temperature change (freezing and thawing), drought, and heavy rain; vegetation or its removal; human or animal activities; variations in water content or pore-water pressure; and wave action. In ultimate limit states, design free water and ground-water levels, or their combination, shall be selected from available hydrological data and in situ observations to give the most unfavourable conditions that could occur in the design situation being considered, and the possibility of failure of drains, filters, or seals shall be considered. The possibility of emptying a canal or water reservoir for maintenance, or due to dam failure, should also be considered; for serviceability limit states, a less severe, more typical water level or pore-water pressure may be used. For slopes along waterfronts, the most unfavourable hydraulic conditions are normally steady seepage for the highest possible ground-water level and rapid draw-down of the free water level. In deriving design distributions of pore-water pressure, account shall be taken of the possible range of permeability anisotropy and variability of the ground.
key_points: Actions per 2.4.2(4); also account for construction processes, new nearby slopes/structures, prior/continuing ground movement, vibration
Also account for climatic variation (freeze-thaw, drought, heavy rain), vegetation, human/animal activity, water content/pore pressure variation, wave action
ULS design water levels: most unfavourable per available hydrological data/observations, including possible drain/filter/seal failure
Consider possible canal/reservoir emptying for maintenance or dam failure; SLS may use less severe, typical water levels
Waterfront slopes: most unfavourable hydraulic condition is normally steady seepage at highest GWT combined with rapid drawdown
Design pore-pressure distributions account for the possible range of permeability anisotropy and ground variability
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the actions and hydraulic design conditions for an overall-stability (slope) analysis, especially waterfront slopes subject to rapid drawdown.

sections.title: Design and construction considerations
sections.summary: Requires that overall stability and ground movement be checked using comparable experience, considering typical structures needing an overall-stability analysis (retaining structures; excavations, slopes, embankments; foundations on sloping/natural/embankment ground; foundations near excavations, cuts, buried structures, or shore). If stability cannot be verified or movements are unacceptable, the site is unsuitable without stabilising measures, which may include concrete cover, gabions, ground nailing, vegetation, or drainage.
sections.body: The overall stability of a site and movements of natural or made ground shall be checked taking into account comparable experience, according to 1.5.2.2. The overall stability and movement of ground supporting existing buildings, new structures, slopes, or excavations shall be considered; where the stability of the ground cannot be clearly verified prior to design, additional investigations, monitoring, and analysis should be specified according to the provisions of 11.7. Typical structures for which an analysis of overall stability should be performed are: ground retaining structures; excavations, slopes, or embankments; foundations on sloping ground, natural slopes, or embankments; and foundations near an excavation, cut, buried structure, or shore. Stability problems or creep movements occur primarily in cohesive soils with a sloping ground surface, although instability can also occur in non-cohesive soils and fissured rocks in slopes where the inclination -- which may be determined by erosion -- is close to the angle of shearing resistance; increased movements are often observed at elevated pore-water pressures or close to the ground surface during freezing and thawing cycles. If the stability of a site cannot readily be verified, or the movements are found unacceptable for the site's intended use, the site shall be judged unsuitable without stabilising measures. The design shall ensure that all construction activities in and on the site can be planned and executed such that the occurrence of an ultimate or serviceability limit state is sufficiently improbable. Slope surfaces exposed to potential erosion shall be protected if required, to retain the safety level; slopes should be sealed, planted, or protected artificially, and for slopes with berms a drainage system within the berm should be considered. Construction processes shall be taken into account as far as they might affect overall stability or the magnitude of movement. Potentially unstable slopes may be stabilised by a concrete cover with or without anchorage, an abutment of gabions (steel net or geotextile cages), ground nailing, vegetation, a drainage system, or a combination of these. The design should follow the general principles of Sections 8 and 9.
key_points: Overall stability and ground movement checked using comparable experience per 1.5.2.2
Where stability cannot be clearly verified prior to design, specify additional investigation, monitoring, and analysis per 11.7

Typical structures needing overall-stability analysis: retaining structures; excavations/slopes/embankments; foundations on sloping/natural/embankment ground; foundations near excavations/cuts/buried structures/shore
Stability/creep problems mainly in sloping cohesive soils, but also non-cohesive soils and fissured rock near the angle of shearing resistance
If stability cannot be verified or movements are unacceptable, the site is unsuitable without stabilising measures
Protect erosion-exposed slope surfaces; seal/plant/protect slopes; drainage system within berms
Stabilisation options: concrete cover (with/without anchorage), gabion abutment, ground nailing, vegetation, drainage system, or combination
Design follows the general principles of Sections 8 (ground anchorages) and 9 (retaining structures)
sections.applicability: Applies to any site where overall (slope-type) stability of natural or made ground must be checked and, if inadequate, stabilised.

sections.title: Ultimate limit state design
sections.summary: Introduces the ULS verification of overall (slope) stability: general stability analysis for slopes using the Annex A partial factors of Table A.3/A.4/A.14 (11.5.1), stability of slopes and cuts in rock masses against translational/rotational/toppling failure and rock falls (11.5.2), and stability of excavations including base heave (11.5.3).
sections.body: This clause covers the ultimate limit state design of overall stability under three headings: 11.5.1 covers the general stability analysis method for slopes in soil, verified in ULS (GEO and STR) using the partial factors of Annex A Tables A.3, A.4, and A.14; 11.5.2 covers the additional considerations needed for slopes and cuts in rock masses, where discontinuities can govern the failure mode; and 11.5.3 covers the stability of excavations, including the bottom heave check that links to Section 10.
key_points: 11.5.1 Stability analysis for slopes: general method, Annex A Tables A.3/A.4/A.14 partial factors
11.5.2 Slopes and cuts in rock masses: translational/rotational failure of blocks/wedges, toppling, rock falls
11.5.3 Stability of excavations: overall stability near the excavation and base heave (links to Section 10)
sections.applicability: Applies to the ULS verification of overall stability for slopes in soil, slopes and cuts in rock, and excavations.

sections.title: Stability analysis for slopes
sections.summary: Requires overall slope stability (including existing, affected, or planned structures) to be verified in ULS (GEO and STR) using design values of actions, resistances, and strengths per the partial factors of Annex A Tables A.3, A.4, and A.14; Design Approach 3 is the design approach normally used for slope/overall-stability analyses (2.4.7.3.4.4 NOTE 2). Covers method selection (circular vs. non-circular, numerical methods), homogeneity assumptions, layered-soil and jointed-material considerations, and the treatment of favourable/unfavourable weight density.
sections.body: The overall stability of slopes, including existing, affected, or planned structures, shall be verified in ultimate limit states (GEO and STR) with design values of actions, resistances, and strengths, where the partial factors defined in A.3.1(1)P, A.3.2(1)P, and A.3.3.6(1)P shall be used; the recommended values for persistent and transient situations are given in Tables A.3, A.4, and A.14 (digitized as table_a_3_str_geo_actions, table_a_4_str_geo_soil_parameters, and table_a_14_slope_stability_resistance, the last giving gamma_R;e = 1,0/1,1/1,0 for R1/R2/R3). Per 2.4.7.3.4.4 NOTE 2, Design Approach 3 (digitized as design_approach_sets('DA3'): structural actions via set A1 or geotechnical actions via set A2, combined with material set M2 and resistance set R3) is generally the design approach used for slope and overall-stability analyses -- structural actions transmitted onto or through the sliding soil mass (e.g. a building load contributing to the driving mass) are treated via the geotechnical action set A2 rather than A1. In analysing the overall stability of soil or rock, all relevant modes of failure shall be taken into account; when choosing a calculation method, the following should be considered: soil layering; occurrence and inclination of discontinuities; seepage and pore-water pressure distribution; short- and long-term stability; creep deformations due to shear; type of failure (circular or non-circular surface, toppling, flow); and use of numerical methods. The mass of soil or rock bounded by the failure surface should normally be treated as a rigid body or as several rigid bodies moving simultaneously, with failure surfaces or interfaces between rigid bodies having a variety of shapes including planar, circular, or more complicated forms; alternatively, stability may be checked by limit analysis or the finite element method. Where ground or embankment material is relatively homogeneous and isotropic, circular failure surfaces should normally be assumed; for slopes in layered soils with considerable shear-strength variation, special attention should be paid to the weaker layers, which may require analysis of non-circular failure surfaces. In jointed materials, including hard rock and layered or fissured soils, the shape of the failure surface can partly or fully be governed by discontinuities, and analysis of three-dimensional wedges should normally be made; if the failure surface cannot be assumed two-dimensional, use of three-dimensional failure surfaces should be considered. Existing failed slopes that could potentially be reactivated should be analysed considering both circular and non-circular failure surfaces, and the partial factors normally used for overall stability analyses may then not be appropriate. A slope analysis should verify the overall moment and vertical stability of the sliding mass; if a method of slices is used and horizontal equilibrium is not checked, the inter-slice forces should be assumed to be horizontal. In cases where a combined failure of structural members and the ground could occur (for example, failure surfaces intersecting piles or flexible walls), ground-structure interaction shall be considered by allowing for the difference in their relative stiffnesses. Since a distinction between favourable and unfavourable gravity loads is not possible in assessing the most adverse slip surface, any uncertainty about weight density of the ground should be considered by applying upper and lower characteristic values of it. The design shall show that ground deformation under design actions due to creep or regional settlement will not cause unacceptable damage to structures or infrastructure on, in, or near the particular ground.
key_points: Overall slope stability verified in ULS (GEO and STR) using Annex A Tables A.3/A.4/A.14 partial factors
Table A.14 (table_a_14_slope_stability_resistance): gamma_R;e = 1,0/1,1/1,0 for R1/R2/R3
Per 2.4.7.3.4.4 NOTE 2, Design Approach 3 (design_approach_sets('DA3')) is generally used for slope/overall-stability analyses, with structural actions on the soil treated via geotechnical set A2
Method selection considers soil layering, discontinuities, seepage/pore pressure, short/long-term stability, creep, failure-surface type, and numerical methods
Homogeneous/isotropic ground: assume circular failure surfaces; layered soils with weak layers may need non-circular surface analysis
Jointed/hard-rock materials: consider three-dimensional wedge analysis; use 3-D failure surfaces where the surface cannot be treated as 2-D
Existing reactivated failed slopes: analyse both circular and non-circular surfaces; the usual partial factors may not be appropriate
Method of slices without horizontal equilibrium check: assume horizontal inter-slice forces
Combined structure-ground failure (e.g. surfaces intersecting piles/flexible walls) requires ground-structure interaction analysis accounting for relative stiffness
Weight-density uncertainty handled via upper/lower characteristic values (favourable/unfavourable split is not meaningful for the sliding mass)
tables: Table A.3: Partial factors on actions/effects of actions (gamma_F/gamma_E) for STR/GEO, sets A1/A2 (table_a_3_str_geo_actions)
Table A.4: Partial factors for soil parameters (gamma_M) for STR/GEO, sets M1/M2 (table_a_4_str_geo_soil_parameters)
Table A.14: Partial resistance factor (gamma_R;e) for slopes and overall stability, sets R1-R3 (table_a_14_slope_stability_resistance)
Design Approach sets (2.4.7.3.4): design_approach_sets('DA3') gives the structural/geotechnical action-set split typically used for slope stability
sections.applicability: Applies to the general ultimate limit state stability analysis of any natural or engineered slope in soil, including slopes affected by or supporting other structures.

sections.title: Slopes and cuts in rock masses
sections.summary: Requires that rock-mass slope/cut stability be checked against translational and rotational failure of isolated blocks or large rock-mass portions, and against rock falls, with particular attention to blocked seepage-water pressure in joints and fissures. Stability analyses rely on reliable knowledge of the discontinuity pattern and shear strength of intact rock and discontinuities; failure modes include sliding, toppling, or a combination, and highly fissured/soft rock may fail along circular or near-circular surfaces through intact rock.
sections.body: The stability of slopes and cuts in rock masses shall be checked against translational and rotational modes of failure involving isolated rock blocks or large portions of the rock mass, and also against rock falls; particular attention shall be given to the pressure caused by blocked seepage water in joints and fissures. Stability analyses shall be based on reliable knowledge of the pattern of discontinuities intersecting the rock mass and of the shear strength of the intact rock and of the discontinuities. Account should be taken of the fact that failure of slopes and cuts in hard rock masses with a well-defined discontinuity pattern will generally involve sliding of blocks or rock wedges, toppling of blocks or slabs, or a combination of toppling and sliding, depending on the orientation of the slope face relative to the discontinuities. It should be considered that failure of slopes and cuts in highly fissured rock masses and in soft rocks and cemented soils may develop along circular or almost circular slip surfaces passing through portions of intact rock. Sliding of isolated blocks and wedges should usually be prevented by reducing the slope inclination through berms, and by installing anchors, bolts, and internal drainage; in cutting slopes, sliding should be prevented by selecting the direction and orientation of the slope face so that movement of isolated blocks is kinematically impossible. To prevent toppling failures, anchoring or bolting and internal drainage should normally be applied. When considering long-term stability of slopes and cuts, the detrimental effects of vegetation and environmental or polluting agents on the shear strength of discontinuities and of the intact rock should be taken into account. In highly fractured rock masses in steep slopes, and slopes susceptible to toppling, spalling, ravelling, and slumping, the possibility of rock falls should always be analysed; where reliable provisions to prevent rock falls are not feasible, rock falls should be allowed to occur with the provision of nets, barriers, or other suitable measures to trap the falling rock. The design of such trapping provisions should be based on a thorough investigation of the possible trajectories of the falling material.
key_points: Check translational and rotational failure of isolated blocks or large rock-mass portions, and rock falls; attention to blocked seepage-water pressure in joints/fissures
Stability analysis requires reliable knowledge of discontinuity pattern and shear strength of intact rock and discontinuities
Hard rock with well-defined discontinuities: sliding of blocks/wedges, toppling of blocks/slabs, or a combination, depending on slope-face/discontinuity orientation
Highly fissured rock or soft rock/cemented soil: may fail along circular or near-circular surfaces through intact rock
Sliding prevention: reduce slope inclination via berms, install anchors/bolts/internal drainage; orient cut faces to make block movement kinematically impossible
Toppling prevention: anchoring/bolting and internal drainage
Long-term stability: account for vegetation and environmental/polluting agents degrading discontinuity and intact-rock shear strength
Analyse rock-fall potential in highly fractured/steep/toppling-susceptible slopes; where prevention is infeasible, provide nets/barriers based on trajectory analysis
sections.applicability: Applies to natural rock slopes and engineered rock cuts where discontinuity-controlled block failure, toppling, or rock fall governs stability, as distinct from soil slope stability in 11.5.1.

sections.title: Stability of excavations
sections.summary: Requires checking the overall stability of ground close to an excavation, including spoil and existing structures/roads/services (per Section 9), the stability of the excavation bottom in relation to design pore-water pressure (per Section 10 for hydraulic failure), and heave of the bottom of deep excavations due to unloading.
sections.body: The overall stability of the ground close to an excavation, including excavation spoil and existing structures, roads, and services, shall be checked (see Section 9). The stability of the bottom of an excavation shall be checked in relation to the design pore-water pressure in the ground; for the analysis of hydraulic failure, see Section 10. Heave of the bottom of deep excavations due to unloading shall be considered.
key_points: Check overall stability of ground near the excavation, including spoil, existing structures, roads, and services (see Section 9)
Check excavation-bottom stability against design pore-water pressure (hydraulic failure analysis, see Section 10)
Consider bottom heave of deep excavations caused by stress relief (unloading)
sections.applicability: Applies to any excavation, particularly deep excavations below the water table, where overall ground stability and unloading-induced base heave must both be verified.

sections.title: Serviceability limit state design
sections.summary: Requires demonstrating that ground deformation will not cause an SLS in structures or infrastructure on or near the ground, considering subsidence causes (ground-water/pore-pressure change, long-term drained creep, soluble-stratum volume loss, mining/gas extraction). Since analytical/numerical prediction of natural-slope deformation is generally unreliable, SLS occurrence should instead be avoided by limiting mobilised shear strength or by monitoring movements and acting to reduce/stop them.
sections.body: The design shall show that the deformation of the ground will not cause a serviceability limit state in structures and infrastructure on or near the particular ground. Subsidence of the ground due to the following causes should be considered: change in ground-water conditions and corresponding pore-water pressures; long-term creep under drained conditions; volume loss of deep soluble strata; and mining or similar works such as gas extraction. Since the analytical and numerical methods available at present do not usually provide reliable predictions of the deformation of a natural slope, the occurrence of serviceability limit states should be avoided by one of the following: limiting the mobilised shear strength; or observing the movements and specifying actions to reduce or stop them, if necessary.
key_points: Design shows ground deformation will not cause an SLS in structures/infrastructure on or near the ground
Subsidence causes to consider: ground-water/pore-pressure change, long-term drained creep, soluble-stratum volume loss, mining/gas extraction
Analytical/numerical natural-slope deformation prediction is generally unreliable
SLS avoidance strategy: limit mobilised shear strength, or monitor movements and act to reduce/stop them
sections.applicability: Applies to serviceability (deformation-based) checks of natural or engineered slopes and the ground supporting nearby structures or infrastructure.

sections.title: Monitoring
sections.summary: Requires ground monitoring with appropriate equipment when calculation or prescriptive measures cannot sufficiently rule out the limit states of 11.2, or when calculation assumptions lack reliable data. Monitoring should provide knowledge of ground-water levels/pore pressures, lateral and vertical ground movements, the depth and shape of a developed slide surface, and rates of movement (with remote readout/alarm where warranted).
sections.body: The ground shall be monitored using appropriate equipment if it is not possible to prove by calculation or by prescriptive measures that the occurrence of the limit states given in 11.2 is sufficiently unlikely, or if the assumptions made in the calculations are not based on reliable data. Monitoring should be planned to provide knowledge of: ground-water levels or pore-water pressures in the ground, so that effective stress analyses can be carried out or checked; lateral and vertical ground movements, in order to predict further deformations; the depth and shape of the moving surface in a developed slide, in order to derive the ground strength parameters for the design of remedial works; and rates of movement, in order to give warning of impending danger -- in such cases a remote digital readout for the instruments or a remote alarm system may be appropriate.
key_points: Monitor the ground with appropriate equipment when calculation/prescriptive measures cannot sufficiently rule out the 11.2 limit states, or assumptions lack reliable data
Monitor ground-water levels/pore-water pressures to support or check effective stress analyses
Monitor lateral and vertical ground movement to predict further deformation
For a developed slide, determine the depth and shape of the moving surface to back-derive strength parameters for remedial-works design
Monitor rates of movement to give warning of impending danger; consider remote digital readout or alarm systems
sections.applicability: Applies when calculation alone cannot adequately demonstrate overall stability, or when an active or developed slide requires movement tracking to support remedial design.
